question.text: Part of the graph of a function $y=f(x)$ with period $4$ is shown above. What is the graph of $y=f(x)$ on the interval $-6 \leq x \leq 6?$
question.explanation:
The graph above shows the function in the interval $-2 \leq x \leq 2.$

Since this interval has length $4,$ and the period of the function is also $4,$ this interval represents a single period of the function.

Therefore, the function will consist of many copies of the shape shown above, shifted horizontally by multiples of $4.$

question.text: The graph of $y = f(x)$ is shown above. Given that $y = f(x)$ is periodic with period $4,$ what is the value of $f(62)?$
question.explanation:
Since the period is $4,$ if we add (or subtract) any multiple of $4$ from the input, the output stays the same.

So, we can keep subtracting $4$ from the input until we get to an input that we see in the graph:

\begin{align} f(62) &= f(62-4)\\[3pt] &= f(62-2\cdot4) \\[3pt] &= \cdots\\[3pt] &= f(62-15 \cdot 4)\\[3pt] &= f(2)\\[3pt] &= 0 \end{align}

question.text: The graph of a periodic function $y = f(x)$ is shown above. What is the period of this function?
question.explanation:
Note that if we shift the graph $3$ units left or right, the graph remains unchanged.

On the other hand, if we shift the graph horizontally by any distance other than $3$ (or a multiple of $3$), we get a different graph.

Therefore, the period of the function is $3.$

question.text: The graph of $y = f(x)$ is shown above. Given that $y = f(x)$ is periodic with period $4,$ what is the value of $f(-46)?$
question.explanation:
Since the period is $4,$ if we add (or subtract) any multiple of $4$ from the input, the output stays the same.

So, we can keep adding $4$ to the input until we get to an input that we see in the graph:

\begin{align} f(-46) &= f(-46+4) \\[3pt] &= f(-46+2\cdot4)\\[3pt] &= \cdots\\[3pt] &= f(-46+11\cdot 4) \\[3pt] &= f(-2) \\[3pt] &= 1 \end{align}
